title: Head lice (pediculosis capitis)
summary: Only a live louse confirms infestation. Wet combing or dimeticone 4% are first-line; permethrin is not recommended in the UK.

glance.think: Scalp itch (or none), nape/behind-ear excoriation, and a live louse found on detection combing.
glance.engine: Pediculus humanus capitis crawls head-to-head; itch is hypersensitivity to saliva. Eggs are cemented to the hair shaft.
glance.backbone: Treat only live infestation. Wet combing or dimeticone 4% (repeat after 7 days); check all household members the same day.
glance.never_miss: No live louse means no treatment. Pubic lice on a child’s eyelashes need a safeguarding pathway.

what: Head lice are scalp infestations with *Pediculus humanus capitis*, a wingless blood-feeding insect about 2–3 mm long. They are commonest in **children aged about 4–11**, especially girls. They are **not a sign of poor hygiene** and do not transmit disease in the UK.

list: Spread is by **direct head-to-head contact**. Lice crawl; they cannot jump, fly or swim. Hats and brushes rarely matter because lice die within about 1–2 days off the scalp.
Females glue eggs near the scalp. Eggs hatch in about 7–10 days; adults live about 3–4 weeks on the host.
**Nits** are empty white egg cases that move out as hair grows. Nits far from the scalp usually mean an old infestation.
Itch may take **4–6 weeks** to appear at first infestation; many children never itch.
Scalp itch (often absent), tickling, and excoriations — especially **behind the ears and at the nape**.
Live grey-brown lice that move away from light; eggs/nits cemented to the shaft.
Complications: secondary impetigo, occipital lymphadenopathy, eczematisation, sleep disturbance and school stigma.

diagnosis: **Only a live louse confirms active infestation (NICE CKS).** Nits alone do not justify treatment.

list: **Detection combing** with a fine-toothed plastic comb on wet conditioned hair (or dry) is more sensitive than looking alone.
Check **all household members** and treat only those with live lice, **all on the same day**.
Nits stay put; dandruff and hair casts brush or slide off.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: Seborrhoeic dermatitis / dandruff
Greasy or flaky scale that brushes off; no lice
Hair casts
Tubular casts that slide along the shaft
Scalp psoriasis
Thick scale beyond the hairline; nail or body plaques
Tinea capitis
Broken hairs, alopecia, black dots; mycology
Impetigo of the nape
Honey crust — look for lice as the driver

management: Treat **only when a live louse is found**. Choice depends on preference, age, asthma/eczema and previous treatment.

head: Option
How to use
Notes
rows: Wet combing (Bug Busting)
Conditioner + detection comb days 1, 5, 9 and 13; check day 17
Suitable for everyone including infants, pregnancy, asthma and eczema
Dimeticone 4% lotion/spray/gel
Dry hair, leave overnight (check product), wash out; **repeat after 7 days**
Physical insecticide; CKS first-line in pregnancy, breastfeeding, young children, asthma/eczema. Flammable while on hair
Isopropyl myristate + cyclomethicone
Short contact (~10 min), comb out; repeat after 7 days
Check age and scalp licence
Malathion 0.5% aqueous liquid
Dry hair, leave 12 h; repeat after 7 days
Only chemical insecticide still recommended; resistance common; aqueous if asthma/eczema

management.title: Not recommended in the UK
management.text: **Permethrin** creme rinses (unsuitable contact time and widespread resistance), shampoos alone, herbal/essential-oil products, electric combs, and “preventive” treatment of people without live lice.

list: Detection-comb 2–3 days after finishing treatment and again after 7 days.
If live lice persist, check technique then switch to a **different mode of action**.
Oral ivermectin or co-trimoxazole for resistant lice are **specialist/off-label** — refer rather than start them yourself.

red_flags: Infant under 6 months (wet combing only; seek advice if this fails).
Extensive secondary infection or severe eczematous scalp.
Pubic lice on a child’s eyelashes → safeguarding pathway.
pearls: There is **no school exclusion** and no need to boil-wash bedding or fumigate. Inform school only as local practice.
Asthma/eczema: prefer wet combing or aqueous dimeticone; avoid alcohol-based lotions.
Itch can persist a few days after cure; leftover nits alone do not mean failure.
UK teaching point: course materials that recommend permethrin for head lice are **out of step with CKS**.
